newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Tension mounts in Serbia as protests roll on.
newsitem.headline: Tension mounts in Serbia as protests roll on.

text.p: Serbia's opposition kept up an unprecedented wave of protests on Thursday as President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist government cracked down on independent media.
Tensions were running high a day after demonstrators threw stones as well as eggs and paint bombs at state television and newspaper offices -- symbols of Milosevic's autocratic rule.
The protesters broke dozens of windows. Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition leaders appealed for calm.
Vuk Draskovic, one of the opposition leaders, told crowds in Belgrade on Wednesday the issue was no longer Milosevic's refusal to accept opposition victories in local elections.
"Until yesterday we fought to protect our election victory. Now the goal of our rebellion is the resignation of Slobodan Milosevic," Draskovic said.
Zajedno has led more than a week of demonstrations since the authorities annulled results of a municipal poll which went badly against Milosevic's ruling Socialists.
Diplomats expressed concern the standoff could turn violent as authorities clamped down on independent radio and newspapers trying to cover the crisis.
The capital's only independent radio station, B-92, said its signal was being repeatedly jammed every time it attempted to broadcast news.
"Our signal has been jammed all day," said journalist Aleksandar Vasovic. "Its OK as long as we broadcast music but as soon as we begin the news programme they start jamming us."
"We still don't know who is jamming us but our technicians strongly believe someone is using a smaller transmitter which is set on our frequency."
The opposition's election victory and the street protests have embarrassed Milosevic as he tries to improve relations with the West and re-cast himself as a "peacemaker".

The United States delivered a "very stiff message to Milosevic and other members of the government about our opposition to what has happened," State Department spokesman Nick Burns said in Washington.
He said U.S. diplomats had urged Miliosevic to overturn the annulment of the opposition victory and warned authorities against any "undue use of force".
University students, who began a strike this week in Belgrade faculties, started another day of marches at midday on Thursday. A larger opposition demonstration was due later.
There was a carnival atmosphere among the students as they made their way through the city, beating drums and singing.
A group of young women gave traffic police flowers which were accepted with a smile. "Bravo, kids, just go ahead", said one of the policemen.
Milosevic brutually crushed similar protests in 1991 with tanks and water-cannons. This time he faces demonstrations in several other towns across the country.
Large numbers of workers have joined rallies in Kragujevac, and Nis, industrial towns that were once Milosevic strongholds.
Up to 80,000 demonstrators marched through central Belgrade on Wednesday. It was one of the largest protests since Zajedno claimed poll victories in 15 of Serbia's 18 biggest towns.
Zoran Djindjic, another opposition leader, told Reuters that Zajedno activists were working with unions to prepare for strikes and civil disobedience.

Re-run elections took place on Wednesday in cities where results 10 days ago were overturned. The opposition urged a boycott in Belgrade, but state media reported the Socialists had secured enough seats to form a majority.
